summary: Describes a Telnet protocol extension that lets the two ends negotiate, coordinate and use Kermit file transfer over an existing Telnet connection. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Two computers already chatting through Telnet can agree to start swapping files using the Kermit method, without making a new connection.

questions: what is the telnet kermit option
subtitle: Letting two Telnet endpoints automatically negotiate and manage Kermit file transfers.

tldr.problem: Starting Kermit file transfers over Telnet requires manual setup where users must coordinate which end is the server and which is the client, introducing timing and dexterity problems.
tldr.mechanism: The KERMIT option (code 47) allows Telnet to negotiate support and use subnegotiations to coordinate Kermit server states, specify the packet start character, and manage client-server relationships.
tldr.outcome: Kermit sessions become embedded within Telnet connections with automatic coordination, so each end always knows whether a Kermit server is available and can restrict commands accordingly.

today: RFC 2840 is an Informational memo describing a Telnet extension for Kermit file transfer. It defines how to negotiate and manage Kermit server availability over Telnet connections.

sections.title: Why Telnet needs Kermit negotiation
sections.content:
The Kermit protocol performs error-corrected file transfer across many connection types and platforms. Traditionally, a user starts the Kermit server on one end and the Kermit client on the other by hand, or runs a script. This works on simple direct-dial connections but creates problems on the Internet: it introduces timing issues, requires manual coordination, and neither end can reliably detect whether the other supports Kermit or knows what mode it is in.

This RFC defines a Telnet option extension so that Telnet itself can manage the negotiation, startup and shutdown of Kermit services on both ends, embedding Kermit sessions within Telnet sessions rather than starting them separately.
sections.eli5: Kermit is a way to send files between computers. Normally the person has to say "Start a Kermit server here" and "Connect to it over there" by hand. This RFC lets Telnet do that automatically.

sections.title: The KERMIT option and negotiation
sections.content:
The option code is KERMIT (47), assigned by IANA. Support for a Kermit server is negotiated separately in each direction using standard Telnet commands: IAC WILL KERMIT (sender has a Kermit server), IAC WONT KERMIT (sender does not), IAC DO KERMIT (request it), and IAC DONT KERMIT (refuse it).

Once both sides agree, subnegotiations control the Kermit server state. START-SERVER (code 0) indicates the server is active and ready to accept Kermit packets; STOP-SERVER (code 1) indicates it is not. The requesting side can send REQ-START-SERVER (code 2) or REQ-STOP-SERVER (code 3) and the server responds with RESP-START-SERVER (code 8) or RESP-STOP-SERVER (code 9) to indicate the resulting state. Each side must send SOP (code 4) to specify the Start Of Packet character (normally SOH, decimal 1) it will use; this allows the other end to recognize Kermit packets in the data stream.
sections.eli5: Telnet uses special codes to ask "Can you speak Kermit?" and to say "I am ready to receive files now" or "I am not ready." The two computers also tell each other what special character marks the start of a Kermit message.

sections.title: Coordinating Kermit server states
sections.content:
When WILL KERMIT is negotiated in a direction, the Kermit server on the WILL side starts in the stopped state. The WILL side sends START-SERVER when it becomes active. If the DO side wants to start the server, it sends REQ-START-SERVER; the WILL side responds with RESP-START-SERVER or RESP-STOP-SERVER to indicate whether the request was granted. When the Kermit server receives a FINISH, REMOTE EXIT or BYE packet from a client, it must send STOP-SERVER. These rules ensure both sides always know whether a server is available and can present the user only with valid commands.

Kermit protocol takes precedence over Telnet: Telnet processes the IAC (decimal 255) byte first. Kermit packets respect Telnet's NVT (Network Virtual Terminal) rules unless Telnet binary mode is negotiated. If binary mode is used, it should be negotiated when entering Kermit protocol and restored when exiting, allowing more efficient transfers.
sections.eli5: One side says "I am starting a Kermit server" by sending a special message. The other side can ask "Can you accept files?" and the first side says yes or no. This way both computers always know which one is ready to send or receive files.

sections.title: Security and implementation notes
sections.content:
Implementors must enforce appropriate user authentication and file system access restrictions in conjunction with their Kermit implementation; these are beyond the scope of the RFC. The option is primarily intended for dedicated Kermit services (such as the Internet Kermit Service on port 1649) rather than traditional Telnet shell access on port 23.

Example 5 in the RFC illustrates a potential deadlock: two Telnet clients that both accept incoming connections and both have active Kermit servers can reach a state where neither is processing input. The RFC therefore mandates that a Telnet partner may not restrict its command set to Kermit-only commands if it accepted the incoming connection, to prevent this deadlock.
sections.eli5: The system using this has to make sure only the right person can send files and that they cannot access files they should not. It also has to avoid a deadlock where both sides are waiting for the other to do something.
